ta-l1d32q2-d1e97.summary: The Prooemium of the second question of Distinction 32 turns to what pertains to the Son and announces two articles: whether the Father is wise by the Son or begotten wisdom, and whether the Son is wise by begotten or unbegotten wisdom.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e109.summary: First argument that the Father is wise by begotten wisdom. Every wise person is wise by his wisdom, and the Son is the wisdom of the Father, the unbegotten wisdom.
claims: The Son is the Father's wisdom.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e112.summary: Second argument. One is wise by the wisdom without which he would not be wise, and without the Son the Father would not be wise (Augustine, Dist. 9).
claims: Without the Son the Father would not be wise.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e115.summary: Third argument. One is wise by the wisdom in which he sees what he knows, and God sees all things in the Word (Augustine, Dist. 31).
claims: God sees all in the Word.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e125.summary: Fourth argument. God would not be wise unless he saw himself, and he sees himself in the Son, as a thing in its image.
claims: God sees himself in the Son.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e128.summary: Sed contra from Augustine in the text.
claims: Augustine denies it.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e131.summary: Thomas's determination. Although the Father speaks himself by his Word, it must in no way be granted that he is wise by begotten wisdom, because of the different modes of signifying. 'Word' signifies by way of operation, which denominates what it proceeds from, so the Father is called speaking by the begotten Word, as loving by the proceeding love. 'Wisdom' is signified as a form remaining in its subject, so someone is called wise only by what is in him, not by what is from him. Whatever is signified as being in something as form, substantial or accidental, is signified as principle of something in it, of being or operation, and since the Son has no character of principle with respect to the Father, the Father is not wise by the Son or begotten wisdom.
claims: The Father speaks by the Word but is not wise by begotten wisdom.
Wisdom denominates as an inhering form, which would make the Son a principle of the Father.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e134.summary: Reply to the first argument. The Father's wisdom is said in two ways: the wisdom in him, essential wisdom, by which he is formally wise; and the wisdom proceeding from him, by which he is not called wise, as a man is not called wise by the wisdom he produces in another by teaching.
claims: The Father is wise by essential wisdom, not by the wisdom proceeding from him.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e137.summary: Reply to the second argument. Augustine there takes essential wisdom, without which the Father would not be wise, as appropriated to the Son by the Apostle (1 Cor. 1:24, 'Christ the power and wisdom of God'), and wisdom as appropriated would not exist if the Son did not, so the Son must be coeternal with the Father, as is the wisdom appropriated to him.
claims: Augustine's argument concerns essential wisdom appropriated to the Son.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e143.summary: Reply to the third argument. Seeing in something is said two ways: receiving knowledge in it (the intellect from sensibles, the possible intellect in the agent intellect's light, the student in the master's word), or beholding a known thing represented in another (the builder seeing his art in the house he makes, someone seeing what he knows in a book). The Father sees nothing in the Son the first way, since he receives no knowledge from the Son, but he does the second way, since he placed the ideas of all creatures in his Word by begetting it.
claims: The Father sees in the Word as in a representation, not as a source of knowledge.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e147.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Some say the Father sees creatures in the Word but not himself, but Thomas sees no reason why, if he sees creatures shining in the Word, he should not much more see himself, most perfectly represented there; nor is it unfitting that he sees himself in creatures, which represent divine goodness by image or vestige. Still it does not follow that the Father is wise by begotten wisdom.
claims: The Father sees himself in the Word, and even in creatures, without being wise by them.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e164.summary: First argument that the Son is not wise by begotten wisdom. The Son is wise by nothing other than the Father, as he is God by nothing other, and the Father is wise by essential wisdom, which is not begotten, as the essence is not.
claims: Son and Father are wise by the same essential wisdom.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e167.summary: Second argument. The wisdom by which someone is wise has some character of principle with respect to him, and the Son is in no way his own principle.
claims: Wisdom is principle of the wise.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e170.summary: Third argument. Lombard says begotten wisdom is the Son's hypostasis, and hypostasis is not signified as form, while denomination is by form.
claims: Hypostasis is not a form.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e173.summary: Sed contra. What is not wise per se is wise only per accidens, and the Son is not wise per accidens, so he is wise per se, and he is begotten wisdom.
claims: The Son is wise per se.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e182.summary: A further question: whether the Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom. Argument against: the wisdom by which one is wise is signified as an inhering form, and the Father is not in the Son as an inhering form, so as the Father is not wise by begotten wisdom, the Son is not wise by unbegotten wisdom.
claims: The Father is not an inhering form in the Son.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e185.summary: Sed contra. One is wise by the wisdom from which he has being wise, and the Son has it from the Father, unbegotten wisdom.
claims: The Son has wisdom from the Father.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e194.summary: Thomas's determination on the first quaestiuncula. The prepositions 'from' (a) and 'through' (per) differ: 'from' designates only efficient principle, 'through' principle in any genus of cause, so whatever is from something is through it but not conversely. In God there can be only two kinds of causal relation: one real, of efficient or originating cause, as the Father is principle of the Son; the other only conceptual, of form, as the Father is God by his deity. So in 'the Son is wise by wisdom' the ablative is construed either as quasi-efficient, and then it is false, meaning he is wise from begotten wisdom, from himself, whereas he has wisdom as being from the Father, unbegotten wisdom, so in this sense he is wise from or through unbegotten wisdom but not from or by himself; or as quasi-formal principle, which is twofold: what follows a form is through that form (man understands through the soul) or through the one having the form (man is rational per se, through what is of his essence). As to what the Son is formally wise by, it is essential wisdom, neither begotten nor unbegotten, so he is wise through and by it, but not from it, since the essence does not beget. As to the one having that form, the Son's hypostasis, also called begotten wisdom, he is wise through begotten wisdom or through himself, by begotten wisdom or by himself.
claims: Efficiently, the Son is wise from unbegotten wisdom, not from himself.
Formally, he is wise by essential wisdom, and per se, through his own hypostasis, begotten wisdom.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e197.summary: Reply to the first argument. 'Wisdom' supposing for the essence cannot be called begotten or unbegotten, but it can supposing for the hypostasis, though it always signifies the essence, as 'God' does (why 'wisdom' admits this supposition more than 'essence' was said in Dist. 5). Though the essence that is Father and Son is the same, the hypostasis is not, so it does not follow that the Father is wise by begotten wisdom, only the Son.
claims: 'Wisdom' can suppose for the hypostasis while signifying the essence.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e200.summary: Reply to the second argument. In what is said per se, something of the thing's essence is principle of what is predicated per se, as rational of man; the supposit need not be its principle except as having or operating. So the Son's hypostasis need not be its own principle; it suffices that what is his essence is the formal principle of being wise, which belongs to the Son, who is wise by the essence he shares with the Father, and so is called wise per se.
claims: Per se predication requires the essence, not the supposit, as principle.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e203.summary: This also answers the third argument.

claims: The Son is wise per se.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e217.summary: Thomas's determination on the further question. The Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom if the ablative is construed as quasi-efficient principle, not if as quasi-formal principle; formally he is wise by essential wisdom, or by himself.
claims: Efficiently the Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom; formally by essential wisdom.

ta-l1d32q2-d1e227.summary: An expositio textus. (1) The opinions on whether the Son is wise per se differ because some took 'per' as designating any principle and others as opposed to 'a' (efficient), designating in God a quasi-formal relation, and so simply granted that the Son is wise per se. (2) Hilary shows from John 14:10 ('the Father abiding in me does the works') that the Son does not act from himself but from the Father in him, and from John 8:29 ('I always do what pleases him') that he acts through himself; he would be weak in not acting from himself unless he had from God the Father to act as a hypostasis subsisting and operating per se. (3) Begotten and unbegotten wisdom are one wisdom as begotten and unbegotten God are one God, by the commonness of the form signified, deity and wisdom, while the distinction of hypostases makes 'begotten' and 'unbegotten'. (4) Love is the whole Trinity, and yet the Spirit is love, because the personal is not counted with the essential, the person not being really distinct from the essence.
claims: The Son acts and is wise per se, though not from himself.
Begotten and unbegotten wisdom are one wisdom; the personal is not counted with the essential.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e159.summary: The first quaestiuncula of Article 2 gives arguments that the Son is not wise by begotten wisdom (shared essential wisdom, wisdom as principle, hypostasis not a form) and the contrary argument that he is wise per se.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e177.summary: The second quaestiuncula of Article 2 asks whether the Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom, with arguments on each side.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e189.summary: Thomas's solution to the first quaestiuncula distinguishes 'from' (efficient) and 'through' (any cause). Efficiently the Son is wise from unbegotten wisdom, not from himself; formally he is wise by essential wisdom and per se, through his own hypostasis, begotten wisdom. 'Wisdom' can suppose for the hypostasis, and per se predication requires only that the essence be the formal principle.
claims: Formally the Son is wise by essential wisdom and per se; efficiently from the Father.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e212.summary: Thomas's solution to the second quaestiuncula holds that the Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom efficiently, not formally.
claims: The Son is wise by unbegotten wisdom efficiently.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium announces two articles on what pertains to the Son: whether the Father is wise by begotten wisdom, and whether the Son is wise by begotten or unbegotten wisdom.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e101.summary: Article 1 holds that the Father is in no way wise by the Son or begotten wisdom, though he speaks by the Word, because wisdom denominates as an inhering form, which would make the Son a principle of the Father, while 'Word' denominates as operation. The Father is wise by essential wisdom, Augustine's argument concerns wisdom appropriated to the Son, and the Father sees all things, and himself, in the Word as in a representation, not as a source of knowledge.
claims: The Father is not wise by begotten wisdom, though he speaks by the Word.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e151.summary: Article 2, in two quaestiunculae, distinguishes efficient from formal construal of 'wise by wisdom'. Efficiently, the Son is wise from unbegotten wisdom, the Father, not from himself. Formally, he is wise by essential wisdom and per se, through his own hypostasis, which can be called begotten wisdom.
claims: The Son is wise from the Father efficiently and by essential wisdom formally, and per se.

ta-l1d32q2-Dd1e222.summary: The Expositio textus explains the opinions on whether the Son is wise per se, Hilary's argument that the Son acts not from himself but through himself, the unity of begotten and unbegotten wisdom, and why the personal is not counted with the essential.
claims: The Son acts per se but not a se.

ta-l1d32q2.summary: Quaestio 2 of Book I, Distinction 32 treats locutions about the Son as wisdom. Article 1 holds that the Father is not wise by begotten wisdom, since wisdom denominates as an inhering form, though he speaks by the Word, which denominates as operation, and he sees all things in the Word as in a representation. Article 2 holds that the Son is wise from unbegotten wisdom efficiently and by essential wisdom formally, and per se through his own hypostasis.
claims: The Father is not wise by begotten wisdom.
The Son is wise from the Father efficiently and by essential wisdom formally.
